name: interface
shows: Saturn up close: along the top, time, the scenarios, eclipses, the sky, the manual and the tools to add bodies; on the right, every body, and the one selected with the physics that moves it

name: solar-system
shows: The real solar system five months after 1 January 2025, with relativistic gravity: the planets' orbits, the asteroid belt and the comets

name: earth
shows: Earth on 1 January 2025: clouds, blue Rayleigh haze, the Pacific in daylight and night falling over Asia

name: saturn-2032
shows: Saturn in April 2032 from below its rings: Cassini's measured ring structure, and Saturn's shadow across the rings

name: belts
shows: The asteroid belt and Jupiter's two Trojan clouds, 60° ahead of and behind it, from 28,331 real orbits, in the glow of the zodiacal dust

name: black-hole
shows: Gaia BH1 from 570 km, nearly edge on to a disk drawn around it: its shadow, with the disk's far side bent over the top and under the bottom by its gravity, rays traced one by one. The disk is an illustration, a thin disk as Novikov and Thorne model one: Gaia BH1 has none that's been seen

name: spinning-black-hole
shows: Cygnus X-1, spinning at 0.9985, from 9° above the disk drawn around it: the shadow flattened where light circles with the spin, and the disk's far side lensed over the top

name: neutron-star
shows: The Hulse–Taylor pulsar from close by: its gravity bends its light, so it looks 1.25 times its size with more than half its surface in view, and its two radio beams
command: cargo run --release -- --add "PSR B1913+16 pair:30" --focus "PSR B1913+16" --zoom 6 --paused --capture neutron-star.png --at 7

name: gravitational-waves
shows: GW150914's two black holes at 20 Hz: their gravitational waves' crests spiral out at the speed of light, and the clock-rate map glows where clocks run slowest
command: cargo run --release -- --add "GW150914 pair:30" --focus "GW150914 heavier hole" --zoom 600 --pitch 60 --paused --overlays waves,clocks,models --capture gravitational-waves.png --at 7

name: tides
shows: Earth's tides and the shape of space around it: arrows stretched toward and away from the Moon and the Sun, and space dipping toward Earth's center

name: eclipse-path
shows: The total solar eclipse of 12 August 2026 at its greatest, found by the eclipse finder in the app's own simulation: the Moon's shadow on Earth and its path of totality

name: totality
shows: The same eclipse from Reykjavík at totality: the Moon's black disk over the Sun, with the corona around it

name: crater
shows: Chicxulub's estimated impactor, sent at Earth: the crater it digs, 25 hours later in the noon Sun
command: cargo run --release -- --add "Chicxulub impactor:0.002@Earth" --aim 12,0.5 --advance 0.00289 --focus Earth --zoom 1.12 --yaw -75 --pitch 39 --speed real --capture crater.png --at 2

name: collision
shows: A second Earth strikes Earth at 30 km/s, a little off center: the fragments it throws off, and what's left
command: cargo run --release -- --add earth:0.0003@Earth --aim 30,0.3 --focus Earth --zoom 330 --speed hour --capture collision.png --at 20

name: alpha-centauri
shows: α Centauri A and B, 4.4 light-years away, on their 80-year orbit
command: cargo run --release -- --focus "Alpha Centauri A" --zoom 4000 --pitch 85 --speed decade --capture alpha-centauri.png --at 4

name: clusters
shows: The Milky Way's globular clusters, and Omega Centauri, the largest

name: milky-way
shows: The Milky Way from 35 kiloparsecs, drawn as light: its disk and bulge, with the Sun on its path round the center

name: scenarios
shows: The Scenarios window: twelve famous events, each played as a film

name: manual
shows: The manual inside the app, at its beginning

name: film
shows: The Hulse–Taylor pulsar's film: the orbit turning as general relativity says, with a card measuring it against the pulsar's timing

name: hulse-taylor
shows: The Hulse–Taylor pulsar's film, its fourth shot: at a month a second, the orbit's closest point turns 4.2° a year, as general relativity says

name: saturn-moons
shows: Saturn's moons at a day a second, each on its own orbit in the plane of the rings
